article.headline: How Freudian Psychic Energy Became the Algorithm That Trains Neural Networks
article.lede: The image @mattecapu shared is a passage from a history of artificial intelligence describing the origins of **backpropagation** — the learning algorithm inside virtually every modern neural network. Its author was not a computer scientist but a Harvard political-science doctoral student trying to formalize Sigmund Freud. The tweet's dry punchline ('never laughing at crackpots again') is, on inspection, a precise historiographic observation.
article.body:
Paul Werbos was working under the political scientist Karl Deutsch at Harvard in the early 1970s when he made the conceptual leap. Freud had described mental associations in hydraulic terms: emotional charge on outcome B flows backward through the associative pathway to source A, in proportion to the strength of that pathway. Werbos noticed this was mathematically identical to what an optimiser needs to do when adjusting a complex system — attribute blame for an error back through every step that produced it. 'That's exactly what backpropagation does,' he later said in a recorded interview. He formalised the insight into what he called the *chain rule for ordered derivatives*, a general theorem for computing how a change at any output should be credited to each input in a nested chain of functions. The result appeared in his 1974 Harvard thesis, *Beyond Regression: New Tools for Prediction and Analysis in the Behavioral Sciences*. The first empirical application was Deutsch's own research agenda: an econometric model predicting nationalism and social communications across countries.

The thesis then largely disappeared. A DARPA-funded 1978 report on conflict forecasting was blocked by the agency before publication. A 1978 journal paper referred to the method but had the explanatory appendix stripped for space. The Department of Energy, where Werbos worked after his doctorate, prevented him from publishing related work until 1988. The first complete, publicly accessible academic presentation of backpropagation applied specifically to neural networks came only at an IFIP conference in 1981, appearing in print from Springer in 1982 — seven years after the thesis and more than a decade after the original insight.

By then, David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams were independently converging on the same mathematics. Their 1986 *Nature* paper, 'Learning representations by back-propagating errors,' arrived at precisely the right historical moment: after the *AI winter*, the extended period of funding collapse and institutional scepticism that followed the failure of early neural-network promises in the 1960s and 1970s. The paper's experiments demonstrated that *multilayer perceptrons* — networks with one or more hidden layers of units between inputs and outputs — could train efficiently, and that those hidden units spontaneously developed useful internal representations of the problem. Rumelhart's group was unaware of Werbos's prior work. The 1986 paper became one of the most cited in computer science; the formulation it popularised is what most practitioners mean today when they say 'backpropagation.'

The history is further complicated by Jürgen Schmidhuber, the Swiss AI researcher who maintains a detailed audit of attribution disputes in the field. Schmidhuber argues that Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 Finnish master's thesis contains *reverse-mode automatic differentiation* — essentially the same mathematical object — with working FORTRAN code, predating Werbos by a year. Werbos's contribution, in Schmidhuber's reading, was the first application to neural networks specifically, not the first invention of the underlying method. The IEEE awarded Werbos its Neural Network Pioneer Award in 1995 explicitly for the discovery of backpropagation, which suggests the engineering community settled the question differently.

What the passage makes vivid — and what the tweet captures — is a recurring pattern in the history of foundational algorithms: the first inventor rarely gets the credit, because the first invention rarely arrives in a form the field can receive. Werbos's work was entangled with political science, Freudian metaphor, and government bureaucracy. Linnainmaa's was a Finnish master's thesis on numerical differentiation. Rumelhart's had the advantage of timing: a community that had just endured years of disappointed expectations and was ready to believe again. The Freudian hydraulics turn out not to have been a detour. They were the path.

concepts.definition: The algorithm used to train neural networks by computing how much each connection weight contributed to the network's error, then adjusting weights accordingly. It works by propagating error signals backward through the network from outputs to inputs, layer by layer, using the chain rule of calculus.

Paul Werbos's formalisation of how gradients — measures of sensitivity — propagate through nested chains of mathematical functions. It generalises the standard calculus chain rule to systems where variables appear in a specific computational order, providing the rigorous foundation for backpropagation.

A neural network architecture with at least one layer of units ('hidden units') between the input and output. Hidden layers allow the network to learn complex, non-linear representations. Training MLPs was the central unsolved problem that backpropagation addressed.

A period of sharply reduced funding and interest in artificial intelligence research, driven by unmet early promises. The most severe ran roughly from the mid-1970s to the mid-1980s, following the 1969 publication of Minsky and Papert's *Perceptrons*, which demonstrated theoretical limitations of single-layer networks.

A technique for efficiently computing the derivatives of a function with respect to all its inputs simultaneously, by a single backward pass through the computation. It is mathematically equivalent to backpropagation and is the foundation of modern deep-learning frameworks.

article.fact_check: The source passage states that 'In 1982, Paul Werbos applied backpropagation to MLPs in the way that has become standard.' This is imprecise. Werbos's 1982 Springer paper (presented at IFIP 1981) was the first published neural-network-specific application of backpropagation, but the formulation that actually became standard pedagogy and practice derives from Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams's independent 1986 *Nature* paper — a separate rediscovery by researchers who were unaware of Werbos's prior work. Werbos had priority of invention; Rumelhart et al. had priority of impact. Most practitioners learned the algorithm from the 1986 paper or its descendants.

poster_mattecapu.blurb: Matteo Capucci is a mathematician and researcher specializing in category theory, applied category science, and the mathematical foundations of machine learning. He posts about category theory, programming languages, and their intersections with AI and cognitive science. His follower count is not notably large but he is respected within niche academic circles.
